I really don't get the negative reviews that some people left. They clearly didn't do their research about what kind of game this is. This isn't a "city builder" in the traditional sense, because the city itself is built with deckbuilding and puzzle solving. One person compared this game to a mobile app, and that isn't exactly a bad thing. 

Because of the local co-op and controller support, my wife and I enjoyed playing versus mode, and experiencing the addicting nature of adding cards and abilities as we leveled up. 

With multiple characters to play (who each have their own abilities and starter cards) and a campaign mode that did a great job at explaining this game, I must once again share my skepticism that people would leave a negative review on a game that provides so much value for $6.99. 

Maybe it isn't for everyone, but I'll be darned if this isn't one of the most incredible local multiplayer, city building, deckbuilding, puzzle solving, strategy RPG-lite that I've ever played!

PS: This game has awesome depth when planning and being competitive, but it is also cathartic in a relaxing way that sim city would often provide. A tile-placement/deck building game with a charming urban development skin. Place positive tiles (parks, stores, etc.) near your residential scoring tiles to clear lines. Place negative tiles (industry, mostly) so they don't hurt your housing, but preferably also in large inter-connected zones to build up development points which allows you to unlock new cards and abilities.

At all times, you're working against a clock - generally speaking, the more positive a tile is, the more funding it takes up. Use up too much funding, and you'll need more points per line before they'll clear. Overuse of high-cost tiles can result in requiring so many points to clear a line that you'll be unable to. Clearing a line without enough points available uses up a life, of which you have a very limited amount.

There's about a dozen different characters, each with their own skill tree that favors certain play styles.

There's also a well-done (but quite punishing to max out) campaign, which has you and the hyper-competent intern working against the well-meaning but entirely incompetent new mayor.

Well worth a look.

Concrete jungle in the simplest terms is a deck building and grid based city building puzzle game where you try to maximize your score or, beat your opponent's score.

I applaud whoever had a hand in the creation of concrete jungle every part of the game feels like it feeds into the fantasy of being a city planner working on their designs at a coffee shop. Which, frankly isn't fantasy I thought I wanted but, apparently it was what I'm missing.

This review is focused on the scoring system of the game with some discussion of other things. There are many other things I like about it but the crux of the game is how crunchy this system is.

That being said if you read this far and go to pick up concrete jungle don't worry about score that much at the start. Trying to clear rows is hard enough while you get used to how the game works but, when you're ready you're free to start experimenting with trying for a high score.

Ok, now onto my real review:

This system somehow makes optimal play in this cozy city builder game feel like a thriller movie. With anticipation climbing as the board fills. Any mistake could end the game but, a good play might net you a new high score. After you send the combo though the game sort of resets. Now you are free to consider your options on a wide open board. As the game goes on the points target for each row increases and your deck improves (hopeful). Eventually you'll run out of lives and be unable to clear a row after that the game will end. The campaign missions usually instead see you working within a limited number of rows cleared and working around pre-built buildings with the amount of stars (1-3) determined by your score. 

Now for some details:
By far the best part of concrete jungle is the scoring system I'll only explain solo mode as (vs mode is equally interesting just scored differently for balance reasons) I'll ignore classic mode because the only difference is you get random buildings instead of building a deck.

When you clear multiple columns at the same time the points multiplier doubles each time you clear an extra column. So for 2 rows you get 20 points but, for a full 7 rows you get 640 points or, 32 times as much! Meaning you are pushed towards playing with all the rows you have (at once) restricting your options as the board fills up and risking a huge mistake where you lose a life (fail to clear a row).
For an example say you clear 7 rows, one at a time, each with 3 points this gets you score 3x3x7 = 63 pretty good? We can do better. If we clear all seven rows at once we instead score 63 + 640 = 703! over 10 times as much just by improving your combo. This is an extreme example but early game you do usually get most of your points from combos since you want to be focusing on tech (which I won't touch because this has to end at some point).

The second genius part is that the score a row gets you (ignoring the combo modifier for a minute which is entirely separate from this) is equal to the points squared! This means clearing a row with 8 points only scores 64 but, 9 points scores 81 (+15 for the last point), 10 points scores 100 (+19), and 11 points scores 121 (+21). Each point gives more value then the last as long as they are in the same row. This pushes you to try and focus on a single or few very high scoring rows. Once again risking losing a life because maybe you can just barely squeeze out a few more points in your best row.
For a crazy example, let's say you reach the game's points cap (99 points) in a column. You score 99x99 or 9801! From a single column. I have done this and it feels great every time. That used to be more then my highest score (on endless solo mode) now gained from just a single column.
What a fiendishly clever game.

This is a strategic "build your highscore" puzzler. Something analogous to turn-based Tetris, but with ever stranger and more convoluted pieces with more and more blocks instead of the game becoming more fast-paced. Where you build a deck of possible pieces you have to place...

The good:
The game has some surprising depth you might not expect from the presentation. There are several strategies and deck styles to pick from, and the freedom to combine things in ways outside what the game designers intended. The campaign is not just a tutorial, but actually challenging. There are no bugs as far as I can tell, and a consistent atmosphere and presentation.

The so-so:
Game lacks a consistent vision of what the gameplay should be. It's a strategy game (especially in versus mode) where observing what your opponent is doing and planning for and reacting to it well matters, but the game only lets you watch the AI play in real time, and you have (as far as I can tell) no way to view their deck, their hand, their tech, etc. outside of just being eagle eyed when watching the play zoom by and remembering the pieces you need. For the depth of the game, I would expect full information reveal during your turn, with the ability to see your opponents cards/card counts etc. (some of which matters for your own cards, e.g. some cards simply won't do anything if you miss that the opponent is outside the conditions). The game also has a (mostly optional) feature where a drawback effect of some cards is that your mouse cursor wiggles when placing buildings. This clashes hard with the turn-based sit-and-think style.

The bad:
The depth _is_ limited, and the replayability then too. There's enough for your money's worth, but it feels like it's just a few modifications away from a decent game you can play over and over over years. The accessibility is clunky, using one of your limited moves by accident is quite easy. Exiting the software ends your current game with no warning. Several game concepts are missing tutorials or any hints as to their true functioning contrary to common sense expectations.

Overall: a mixed bag, but probably worth the price and then some - just don't have too high expectations, and you'll enjoy it for what it is with only a few annoyances.

It's not a city builder. It's a deck-building puzzle game in which the cards just happen to be represented by buildings. It's all strictly flavour - you're not dealing with economy, infrastructure, the needs of residents or anything like that. Instead, you're placing pieces in a grid so they'll interact in a way that gives you points, which allows you to clear a row and move onto the next. Because rows are constantly disappearing and taking your buildings with them, you're not making long-term decisions or watching your city evolve, which is a defining point of the city building genre.

It's good for what it is, but I personally didn't have much patience for it. In the two hours that I played I was limited to the top two cards in my hand, which seemed unnecessary, and I couldn't help but feel it was unfair at times. I also couldn't work out how to purchase skills that cost more than one point, but I was probably just missing something.

Even though it wasn't to my taste, my gut tells me that this game is worth recommending. Just don't expect a city builder, because you're not going to get it.

It's not exactly a city builder, so much as it's a deck building game that's all about acquiring points on a map. 

You receive cards which modify the status of the map grid, adding and subtracting point values to locations. These points are captured by specific card placements followed by "clearing" a column, which also opens up a new part of the map while clearing the old. In this you also get points to spend on new cards.

The graphics are pleasant, the music is good, and its got relatively compelling gameplay. The campaign is the right amount of challenging (so far). 

The mixed side is that gameplay is highly subject to the random nature of card draws, and the "story" such as it is, is mostly a distraction. Its tutorial is also a mixed bag, so learning to play is a lot of trial and error, particularly understanding the "block" mechanic which is occasionally counter-intuitive.

Concrete Jungle's an isometric puzzle game disguised as a city-builder.  Now when I say puzzle game, I feel I should clarify, I mean of the "Arcade" variety, not unlike Tetris.  It's easy to learn, difficult to master, and pretty addictive; play it forever.

In Concrete Jungle you take on the role of a city planner, placing down buildings, creating blocks.  Your ultimate goal is to drive up the property value of certain tiles, whose points you collect by placing down homes.  Hit the target, win the column, rinse, repeat.  Clear several columns in a row for a bonus.  If you can't clear a column, sorry, game over (though expert play can earn you a life).

The game comes with a campaign to teach you the ropes and unlock new characters, each with their own playstyle.  It's a tidy presentation with an understated charm.  I cleared the whole thing in about 20 hours.  Then I bought the game again on my phone so I'd have something to play on the subway.

Fun strategy game, but not really a city builder. The city building is just a skin over the turn based Tetris-like building placement/column clearing mechanics. It does scratch the same iches as Tetris, match 3, collectable card games, and to a lesser extent, city building games - so I do recommend it. My 26.6 hrs play time is totally accurate.

It does lack a few key things though that I would like to see in a patch/expansion or sequel - there's no networked multiplayer, just local hotseat style. 

Also while you can turn on a view that shows you all the buildings you've place behind you, it really emphasizes the fact that the game is played on a 8xN tile grid, which looks nothing like a proper city. I think it would be neat if the game changed direction sometimes or maybe even looped back and skimmed your old building placement, so that you would end up with properly shaped city while still keeping the row clearing gameplay. 

Last but not least the amount of time the AI takes to think on its turns can be a bit long sometimes, but at least the AI is challenging.

I recommend this game to anyone that enjoys tile placement mechanics, such as those seen in Civ6, Carcassonne, etc, as well as fans of strategy or puzzle games in general.

Но учтите, игра может начинаться, как примитивное набивание очков, но уже спустя несколько миссий превратится в напряженное и комплексное соревнование, где можно сидеть и думать над размещением каждого здания несколько минут. 
Видов зданий и эффектов множество, заявлено больше 200 и я далеко не все еще открыл. А еще это все объединяется в блоки, бафается/дебафается, карты сбрасываются, тасуются, подбрасываются оппоненту. Всякие подляночки, способности, пропуски и дополнительные ходы... но при этом игровой процесс остается весьма понятным и невязким, не скатывается в нудноту, броски кубиков и чтение.
Милая рисованная графика, приятные треки, смена погоды и времени суток - в игре очень приятно находиться, приятно думать на следующим (тремя, пятью) ходом.

Concrete Jungle is like Tetris, Sim City, and tabletop deckbuilder games all rolled up into one package.

This weird mash-up is why I like this game so much. Instead of yet another match 3 game, Concrete Jungle is a fun, light, casual/puzzle game with a surprising amount of complexity to offer.

Essentially, you are building a deck of cards that represent buildings to add to your city. Some cards generate points, while others collect points. However, points are only collected when a row in your city grid is complete. Once you finish a row, everything in your city slides down and you move on to the next row.

It is so deceptively simple. Easy to get into thanks to well designed tutorial and campaign. But even after the campaign is over, it is easy to get lost in the other casual free play modes. 

Playing the campaign also allows you to unlock new characters to play as which come with new starter decks and progression trees to unlock new advantages during play.  Each one has such a different play style, so there's so much replayablity here.
It's hard but it's fun

The Campaign is ok. It is frustrating to play vs the AI. It was such a downer when I met the AI for the first time, I wanted to give this game a thumbs down. But after a bit attitude readjustment, I managed to complete the campaign. The Custom game is what makes me return to the game. I just love the endless mode, where I can build without any AI interruptions. And it is so satisfying to fill an entire block with high value land all over.

The combinations of starting hands, player characters and deck building with random cards gives this a lot of replayability.

The audio and visuals is over the top for a game like this. Very detailed buildings, fitting ambient sound and music. And the gui is very functional. I miss an in-game reference guide for the certain aspects of the game. I still haven't figured out some of the mechanics and limits.
A very fun game.
